subject: Oracle booked $664B of AI work and burned cash doing it
bodyMarkdown:
Oracle told investors on Thursday night that it is sitting on $664 billion of signed cloud work, and that it burned cash during the quarter building the capacity to deliver it. If you hold a US index fund in an RRSP or a TFSA, you own a slice of that bet whether you picked it or not.

## What Oracle reported

Revenue came in at $19.3 billion, up 30% from a year ago, and cloud infrastructure revenue rose 121% to $7.4 billion. The figure everyone quoted was **remaining performance obligations**, which is the dollar value of contracts signed but not yet delivered, and it hit $664 billion, up $209 billion from a year earlier and $26 billion from where it stood in June. Oracle said more than $30 billion of new AI cloud contracts closed in the quarter alone. Investing.com reported on Thursday that the company guided to at least $90 billion of revenue for the full fiscal year, about 34% growth in constant currency. The company also expects roughly half of that backlog to convert into actual sales over the next 36 months, which means the other half sits somewhere past 2029.

## The gap between a backlog and a bank account

Capital spending was $28 billion in the quarter, and erp.today reported that free cash flow landed at negative $5 billion. Oracle guided to $90 billion to $95 billion of capital spending for the year and said it plans to raise about $40 billion through debt and equity in fiscal 2027, including a $20 billion at-the-market share sale it already completed. Put those beside each other. The revenue is a promise spread over years, while the chips, the buildings and the power hookups get paid for now. Demand looks real to me, and it is the financing I would watch, because a plan like that assumes nothing goes wrong for three years running. A backlog is not collateral. Nobody can repossess a contract that a customer stops being able to fund.

## Adobe, on the other side of the same trade

Adobe reported the same evening. Revenue of $6.76 billion, up 13%, adjusted earnings of $6.13 a share, both ahead of what analysts expected, and it raised its full-year outlook. Its AI-first annual recurring revenue passed $650 million, more than 150% higher than a year ago, and its free creative apps crossed 100 million monthly users. The stock still fell about 2% after hours, Investing.com reported, on questions about turning free users into paying ones. Adobe also said Anil Chakravarthy takes over as chief executive on December 1, with Shantanu Narayen moving to executive chair. Two AI reports on one evening, two verdicts. Investors are paying up for the companies renting out compute and marking down the ones that have to sell software into a market where the tools keep getting cheaper.

## The takeaway

The number I will look for next quarter is Oracle's free cash flow, which was negative $5 billion this time, and how much of that $40 billion raise arrives as debt rather than shares. Borrowing costs on data centre debt will tell you more about where this cycle is heading than the next model launch will. If you own a broad US index fund, look up how much of it is four or five AI infrastructure names before you call yourself diversified. Adobe's new chief executive starts December 1, and Oracle reports again in December.
